narrative_purpose: Show the archetypal pioneer that kick-started Mount St. Helens' pumice plain: one lupine cushion building an island of fertile soil on sterile ground through nitrogen fixation.
subject: A single low cushion of a purple-and-blue flowering lupine plant growing alone on a vast expanse of pale grey volcanic pumice, its roots spreading into the coarse grit, a little dark windblown organic debris caught and trapped around its base making a small darker patch of forming soil.
scene: An endless flat sterile pumice plain under a dim sky, the single lupine the only living thing, bare grey grit stretching to a hazed horizon.
camera: Low three-quarter shot close on the lupine cushion with the empty plain receding behind.
light: Soft diffuse daylight; the lupine carries a faint living teal-green vitality against the dead grey; no strong warm light.
palette: Pale stone-grey pumice dominant, living teal-green and a touch of cool violet on the flowers, dark trapped detritus at the base.
style: Painterly naturalist plate, tender and specific, a portrait of one plant against emptiness.
detail_level: High detail on the lupine and the small darker soil patch it is building; plain dissolves to haze.
composition: The lupine low and slightly off-centre, huge empty pumice negative space around it to stress its isolation.
consistency_notes: ONE isolated pioneer plant on bare pumice, not a field of flowers. The story is a single colonist building the first patch of soil. Grey sterile ground with living-teal plant accent.
negative_prompt: no text, no lettering, no numbers, no labels, no meadow, no dense vegetation, no 3D-render or photographic look, no cartoon style
